 COLUMBIA — Dropping temperatures almost always mean increased utility bills — but there are ways for mid-Missourians to offset those rising costs.
 According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration’s 2025–26 winter fuels outlook , 46% of Americans heat their homes using natural gas and 43% heat their homes using electricity. The administration predicts that the average electricity bill will rise about 4% from November through March 2026, for a national average of about $1,130.
 Columbia Utilities Assistant Director and Vice President Gwen Corches said the department often gets questions from residents about bills this time of year.
 “A lot of definitely bill inquiries... why is the bill going up?” Corches said.
 The city of Columbia, Ameren Missouri and Central Missouri Community Action are some organizations that provide resources to help Missourians pay their utility bills throughout the year.
 Rising winter utility bills may be a concern for some. Income-eligible utility assistance programs are available in mid-Missouri.
 KOMU 8/File 
 City of Columbia utility assistance 
 The city of Columbia offers utility assistance through a monthly lottery for seniors, people with disabilities and families with children age 18 or younger. 
 Income must be at or below 200% of the federal poverty level. Residents can find details about eligibility requirements on the city's website and can apply for programs through the My Key portal .
 The application period for each year is Sept. 1-Aug. 31. Applications will be processed within 30 days, according to the city's website.
 Applicants must be permanent residents of Boone County, or a Boone Electric customer who meets all other eligibility criteria .
 The city also offers budget billing to all customers.
 “That kind of balances your bills across the entire the year; (they) might be a little less when those expensive months happen — it's just balanced out by paying a little bit more in the spring," Corches said.
 How to winterize your home to save money ahead of colder temperatures 
 Columbia Utilities experts share recommendations on how to winterize your home to help you save money.
 Eligibility for budget billing includes having 12 months of continuous service at the customer's current location with no disconnections, returned payments or have no more than three late payments. Applicants must also have a metered service with the city of Columbia Utilities.
 Residents can check their eligibility through the city's website , where they can also apply for budget billing .
 The city also offers free in-home energy assessments through Columbia Power Partners, where specialists help identify parts of a home that would benefit most from upgrades, including insulation levels and HVAC equipment age, according to the city's website.
 Free in-home energy assessments can be requested through the city's website .
 Ameren Missouri 
 Page Selby, manager of customer advocacy at Ameren, said many households don't know when their next financial squeeze could happen. 
 “(They're) one car repair, or one emergency away from being able to have to make some tough choices with our household budgets,” Selby said.
 Ameren offers programs including Clean Slate, Keeping Current and Dollar More.
 “Eligibility is going to be based on income... for Ameren programs we’ve increased that eligibility to 300% of federal poverty level,” Selby said.
 Ameren's Keeping Current  program includes a monthly bill credit, along with help to reduce the total amount owed.
 Those wanting to apply to the program can print out the application and either take it to a local agency or mail it in.
 Ameren's Clean Slate program is available for gas customers who have past due accounts.
 “Our clean slate program allows a customer to pay or get a pledge for 10 percent for their gas bill, and we pay off the rest of it with those program funds" Selby said.
 Residents can go to Ameren's website  to find eligibility requirements for the Clean Slate program. Nine agency partners across Missouri are also available to help with the application process.
 Ameren partners with Central Missouri Community Action  to provide energy assistance funding.
 “They are great partners... and they have a weatherization program that combines not only department of energy funds, but also Ameren funds. And we’ve been able to fund that program at a higher level the last two years,” Selby said.
 Watch the KOMU 8 First Alert Winter Weather Special 
 Central Missouri Community Action  
 Central Missouri Community Action offers the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program or LIHEAP .
 LIHEAP serves the following counties: Audrain, Boone, Callaway, Cole, Cooper, Howard, Moniteau and Osage.
 There are two components of LIHEAP: energy assistance and the energy crisis intervention program. The benefit amount is based on household size, household income, and the type of energy source used in the home, according to CMCA's website.
 Eligibility requirements for LIHEAP include having $3,000 or less in bank accounts, retirement accounts, or investments. Customers must also meet specific income guidelines that vary according to household size and fuel type. Specific income guidelines for application eligibility can be found on Central Missouri Community Action's website .
 The energy assistance program is a one-time payment for heating or cooling costs from October through May. The energy crisis intervention program pays the total amount due on a customer's account, rounded to the nearest dollar, only if the customer is in threat of disconnection, or currently without services. The customer's account much be active.
 Residents wanting to submit their information to the LIHEAP program can fill out an online form . Online applications can be submitted through the Missouri Department of Social Services .
 Disabled and elderly (age 60 or older) households may submit applications as early as Oct. 1. For all other households, the program begins Dec. 1, and applications are accepted beginning Nov. 1. The program officially begins Nov. 1.
 CMCA helps more than 9,000 mid-Missouri families annually by restoring or maintaining their utilities through LIHEAP, according to their website. 
 “If you’re income qualified, reach out to us at CMCA,” said Ben Burgett, CMCA's Director of Housing Development and Weatherization Programs.
 CMCA's Weatherization Assistance program is funded by the U.S. Department of Energy, the Missouri Department of Natural Resources and Ameren Missouri, according to previous KOMU 8 reporting .
 “We’ll send out an energy auditor to your home, they’ll do a full energy assessment,” Burgett said. If an applicant is determined eligible, they are placed on a waiting list. Then, an auditor inspects the apartment, house or mobile home and makes recommend weatherization improvements. They will check the home's air-tightness, air quality, insulation, refrigerator, water heater, HVAC system and gas appliances."
 A contractor is assigned to make the recommended improvements and an inspector will ensure the improvements were completed properly, according to CMCA's website .
 Eligibility for the Weatherization Assistance program is based on total household income and family size which cannot exceed the 200% federal poverty income guidelines.
 Residents can print out the application for the program, and either drop it off or mail it in.
 Ameren's Dollar More Program  
 For those who are financially able to help, Ameren offers the Dollar More program, which allows Missourians to add $1 to their energy bill each month to help others in need.
 Donations to Dollar More are accepted through an Ameren customer's online account, by calling 1-800-552-7583, completing the contribution form and sending via email, mail or fax, or making a one time donation . All donations are tax deductible, according to Ameren's website. 
 “100% of those funds go to helping people in need,” Selby said.
 Residents can request assistance from the Dollar More program if they have income at or below 300% of the Federal Poverty Level.
 Those wanting to apply to the program can reach out to a local agency partnered with the Dollar More program.
